newsitem.title: BELGIUM: UK wait-and-see on EMU unchanged - Kenneth Clarke.
newsitem.headline: UK wait-and-see on EMU unchanged - Kenneth Clarke.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Monday dismissed as preposterous a report his government was about to ditch its wait-and-see stance on a single European Union currency.

At a meeting of EU finance ministers in Brussels, Clarke said that exercising Britain's opt-out now would be "no way to fight an election nor present yourself to the country as a governing party at all".

The comments, made to BBC radio, were widely viewed in Brussels as the closest the pro-European Chancellor of the Exchequer has come to threatening to resign if his Conservative Party shifts its policy in a more "Euro-sceptic" direction.

Clarke was reacting to a British newspaper report that Prime Minister John Major had the backing of 18 of his 22-member cabinet for a policy shift to fight the coming general election on a pledge not to scrap the pound sterling.
Denying that such a move was in the cards, Clarke said it would be senseless.
In Lisbon, where he was attending the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe summit, British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind also denied a policy shift was in the works.
"I have no reason to believe it (the Conservative policy) is going to change," Rifkind said.
Britain negotiated in the EU's Maastricht Treaty the right to opt out of the single currency.
"To give up the right to choose would be to give away the advantage that we gained at Maastricht," Clarke told reporters after the EU meeting.

He repeated the ruling Conservative government's position that a decision would be made only when it was clearer what the economic circumstances of monetary union would be and which countries would take part.
"The policy remains perfectly clear," he said.

But Clarke also said he had secured language in an EU agreement about the legal basis for the single currency, or Euro, that would exempt Britain from regulations concerning the money if it opted out.

"I got wording that completely answered the groundless fears of the House of Commons," he said, referring to concerns by anti-EU members of Parliament that Britain would be bound by rules for a currency it did not have.

Since the opposition Labour party adopted an identical stance to the Conservatives last month, Major has come under growing pressure from "Euro-sceptics" in his deeply divided party to adopt a more distinctive policy in time for the election.
Labour enjoys a lead in opinion polls of about 20 percentage points. The election must be held by May 22.
